title: Using Redis Connection Pools with Lavik 0.1.0
summary: Keep your Redis client while moving value capacity to NVMe SSD. Choose the right routing mode, initialize pooled connections consistently, and size concurrency for the application.

blocks.text: Keep the client. Expand the dataset.

A growing Redis dataset should not force you to redesign every application connection. Lavik 0.1.0 speaks RESP2 and RESP3, keeps a compact index in memory and stores values on NVMe SSD. Your Redis client remains the application entry point. For a service using a connection pool, the integration work is to select the right client mode and preserve clear ownership of each connection.
Choose the routing model before the pool size

Managed Single gives the application one Group covering the keyspace, all 16 logical databases and no Cluster-style MOVED routing. Managed Cluster uses DB0 and Redis Cluster routing, including same-slot rules for multi-key requests. Match the client’s standalone or Cluster connection model to that deployment. This decision determines discovery and routing; adding more pooled sockets does not change it.

Lavik starts a connection with RESP2 semantics and supports RESP3 negotiation. Authentication, the selected database and transaction state belong to the connection. Configure initialization in the client’s connection-creation path so replacement sockets receive the same protocol, authentication and database settings. Keep requests that require a particular connection state on a connection whose lifecycle the client owns explicitly.

Pipelines and ordinary request pools have different reply-consumption rules. When several requests share a socket over time, each caller must consume its replies before another caller takes ownership. After a timeout with an unresolved reply, discard or drain the connection using the client library’s supported behavior. Treat retries of a mutation as an application decision: a local timeout alone does not establish whether the server applied the write.
Give long-lived work its own connection lifecycle

Pub/Sub subscriptions and blocking requests can occupy a connection much longer than a profile lookup. Keep those lifecycles separate from a pool intended for short request-response work. Lavik maintains subscriber state on the connection’s worker and bounds subscriber output; the application should handle reconnection and subscription restoration through its client library.

A connection pool is a concurrency limit, not a capacity plan. Lavik’s worker scheduling and asynchronous storage path overlap independent requests with I/O. In the October 13 SPDK report, Lavik 0.1.0 reaches 1,145.8k peak GET QPS at 1,280 connections over 10 million 1 KiB values. That is a benchmark operating point, not a recommendation to create 1,280 sockets per application. Start with your service’s total in-flight requests, response-time budget and number of application instances.

As the retained dataset expands, keep connection demand and value capacity separate. More historical profiles or cached objects can add stored bytes without adding the same proportion of simultaneous requests. Lavik places those values on NVMe SSD while retaining the Redis-compatible access path. Increase pool size when measured concurrency requires it, and size the index, storage and replica budget for the data you want to retain.
Bring one request path to Lavik

Start a Lavik 0.1.0 instance, choose a client configuration from the current manual, and connect one application path in a staging environment. Keep its existing pool limits for the first comparison. Check normal reads and writes, a replaced connection and recovery after a client timeout; then tune concurrency with the application’s latency metrics. For an existing Redis dataset, the RedisShake guide supplies the full-copy, catch-up and cutover procedure.
